item.title: Australia’s energy transition should reward flexibility, not just generation
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Most of the debate about Australia's electricity transition is about what to build: more wind and solar, more transmission, more storage. All of it is needed, but a grid that runs largely on weather-dependent generation also needs something less visible: the ability to adjust at short notice when electricity is scarce or abundant.
item.content:encoded:
Flexibility means temporarily reducing or shifting electricity use, or dispatching stored or generated energy, when the system needs it.

A manufacturer might slow part of a process without impacting production, a water plant might shift a pumping schedule while still meeting reservoir targets. A site with a battery might draw on it instead of the grid. Large electricity users, in other words, can help stabilise the grid rather than simply adding to demand.

The Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) 2026 Integrated System Plan shows why this matters. Under its optimal development path, most of the remaining coal fleet would withdraw by 2038. By 2050 the plan has nearly 50 GW of dispatchable storage and hydro, including existing hydro, and 17 GW of flexible gas. It also describes demand-side flexibility as a valuable way to support reliability.

This model doesn’t replace new generation, transmission or storage. Flexible demand is a complement: capacity that already sits inside connected businesses and can respond quickly without necessarily building anything new.

There are several ways flexibility can be paid for, and they are not interchangeable. The Wholesale Demand Response Mechanism lets large electricity users, through a registered provider, be paid for reducing consumption against a baseline.

Frequency control ancillary services (FCAS) are 10 separate markets that pay enabled providers to help hold system frequency steady, with the fastest responding within a second. Emergency reserves, contracted by AEMO under the Reliability and Emergency Reserve Trader, are a backstop, used when a shortfall is forecast and the market has not resolved it.

At state level, South Australia’s Firm Energy Reliability Mechanism has begun contracting long-duration firm capacity under its own criteria.

Each of these mechanisms has distinct eligibility and operating requirements, so a site that suits one may not qualify for another. Even a site that is technically able to respond may not be eligible under the rules, or may be eligible but have no commercial route to take part.

For an eligible business, participation can add a revenue stream from assets it already owns. But not every load can be interrupted, and some processes cannot be paused without consequences for safety, product quality or output.

Those limits have to come first. Technology’s role is to make participation practical within them: monitoring the site, responding to dispatch, demonstrating compliance and reconciling settlement.

The gap between what a site can technically do and what the rules allow is where useful flexibility gets lost. Complex industrial sites are a clear example.

Under the National Electricity Rules, only sites with a single connection point can take part in the Wholesale Demand Response Mechanism. The restriction exists for a reason: a site could cut demand at one connection point while raising it at another, showing a reduction that never happened. However, it also excludes multi-connection sites whether or not that risk could be measured and managed.

Regulators are testing an alternative. In June, the Australian Energy Regulator granted trial waivers of up to five years to two demand response providers, VIOTAS Australia (now PowerSync) and one other, each allowing up to 10 multi-connection sites into the mechanism, with response measured across every connection point and regular public reporting.

The trials are meant to inform the Australian Energy Market Commission, which recommended last year that a rule change request to widen eligibility be assessed.

Wider participation will not fix reliability or lower bills on its own, and it should not be sold that way. What it can do is give the market operator more options to balance the system, and give businesses a way to diversify revenue from assets they have already paid for.

Three principles would help energy market bodies and policymakers get this right. Rules should be proportionate: where a risk can be measured and managed, manage it rather than exclude the site. Performance should be measurable: flexibility should be paid for what it verifiably delivers. And market access should be fair: eligible flexible capacity should be able to compete across wholesale demand response, frequency control and emerging state capacity schemes, with clear pathways for complex sites.

Businesses have a part to play too. The first step is to find out whether existing loads, batteries and on-site assets can safely take part.

While Australia keeps building new supply, it should also reward the capacity it already has for responding when it counts.

Author: David Naismith, founder and Chief Executive Officer, PowerSync Technologies

item.title: APA begins solar and battery build in Queensland’s northwest
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Gas pipeline giant APA Group has launched construction of its Sybella Creek solar and battery project in northwest Queensland with full operation targeted for mid-2028.
item.content:encoded:
APA Group, Australia’s largest listed gas infrastructure owner and operator, announced that construction has officially commenced on the $259 million (USD 171.6 million) Sybella Creek solar farm and battery project being built near Mount Isa in Queensland’s northwest.

The project comprises 72 MW of solar generation alongside a 52 MW / 104 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) and will connect to the North West Power System, the APA-operated electricity network that services the towns of Mount Isa and Cloncurry, along with surrounding mining operations and communities.

“As the first large-scale battery energy storage system in the North West Power System, the project will strengthen energy security and support the region’s transition to lower-emission energy sources,” APA has said.

The Sybella Creek project is being built on land alongside APA’s operating 88 MW Dugald River Solar Farm which means facilities such as the switchyard, ancillary buildings, and maintenance facility can be shared.

APA is developing the project under a long-term Energy Supply Agreement with Ernest Henry Mining, a wholly owned subsidiary of Evolution Mining, that operates a copper-gold-silver mine in northwest Queensland.

Engineering group UGL has been awarded the engineering design, procurement, construction and commissioning contract for the project.

For Sydney-based APA, which owns and operates more than 15,000 kilometres of gas pipelines, the Sybella Creek project is part of a shift towards renewable energy, with Sydney-based company building a portfolio of contracted power generation including 340 MW of solar, 342 MW of wind, and 35 MW of BESS.

Construction of the Sybella Creek solar and battery project is expected to wrap up in early 2028 with APA targeting energy supply from about the middle of that year.

item.title: JinkoSolar claims 35.24% efficiency for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell
item.dc:creator: Emiliano Bellini
item.description: The result was confirmed by the Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese solar module manufacturer JinkoSolar has announced that it has achieved a power conversion efficiency of 35.24% for a perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell.

The company said the result was certified by the Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). JinkoSolar previously achieved an efficiency of 34.82% with the same cell configuration.

“This efficiency breakthrough was made possible by multiple core technological innovations, including selective passivation technology for textured silicon surfaces in N-type TOPCon, a perovskite multi-component crystallisation synchronisation control strategy, and nanoscale interface passivation materials and light-management enhancement technologies,” the company said in a statement, adding that the efficiency improvement was achieved over five months.

The company did not disclose further technical details about the cell or the efficiency improvement.

The current world record for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell efficiency is held by Chinese manufacturer Longi, which achieved 35.5% efficiency in July 2026. The result, obtained with a two-terminal tandem cell, was independently certified by the European Solar Test Installation (ESTI). It surpassed Longi’s previous certified record of 34.85%, announced in April 2025.

Longi also recently reported an efficiency of 35.31% for a tandem cell incorporating specially designed self-assembled molecules. Longi previously achieved a certified efficiency of 34.85% in April 2025 and an efficiency of 34.3% for a large-area tandem cell measuring 261 cm².

In January 2026, Chinese module maker Trinasolar achieved 32.6% efficiency for a large-area tandem cell developed with Huairou Laboratory, with the result certified by Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE).

From pv magazine Global

item.title: South Australia cuts rooftop solar after storm sparks power outages
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Owners of rooftop solar systems on South Australia’s Eyre Peninsular have been asked to switch off their inverters after a storm brought down transmission towers in the region, triggering widespread power outages and prompting the state government to declare a state of emergency.
item.content:encoded:
The South Australian government has declared a state of emergency after a “significant” storm cell caused catastrophic damage to electricity transmission infrastructure across the Eyre Peninsula and West Coast, interrupting electricity supply to thousands of customers across the region.

“Severe weather on Thursday 19 November 2026 has caused significant damage to electricity transmission infrastructure, including the destruction of two transmission towers on the 132 kV line between Cultana and Port Lincoln,” the declaration says. “The damage has disrupted electricity supply to communities across the central and lower Eyre Peninsula and West Coast.”

Transmission network operator Electranet said about 24,000 customers across the region had lost power. In an update issued on Friday, it said local generation had restored power to many customers but approximately 10,000 properties on the Eyre Peninsula were still in the dark, warning electricity restoration could take several days as emergency crews work to establish backup supply.

South Australia Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis declared an electricity supply emergency under the Energy Management Act 2004 to support the coordinated response and restoration of electricity supply to affected communities.

The declaration, that will remain in force for 14 days unless revoked earlier, gives the government power to use a diesel generator in Port Lincoln and instructs the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) to “seek spare generation.”

Koutsantonis said ElectraNet and electricity distributor SA Power Networks (SAPN) were working to restore electricity supply as safely and quickly as possible.

The state is also asking households in the Port Lincoln region that have already had their power restored to switch off their rooftop solar systems until advised otherwise by SAPN to avoid tripping the temporary generators supplying them.

“Given Pt Lincoln is now “islanded” from the NEM, we are asking people in that region with solar panels to safely turn them off because they could trip the temporary generators supplying the township,” Koutsantonis said.

“Please go to the SAPN website and follow the instructions to safely turnoff your solar array. This advice does not apply to rest of the state.”

ElectraNet said its crews are working around the clock to restore transmission services as quickly and safely as possible.

“This involves engineering and constructing temporary solutions to restore transmission supply while the damaged infrastructure is repaired,” it said. “Given the extent of the damage, some communities could remain without power for several days.”

The event has triggered memories of the 2016 blackout when South Australia suffered a statewide blackout.

In that event, a storm damaged critical transmission infrastructure in the state’s Mid North, triggering a cascading failure across the electricity system that caused South Australia to separate from the broader National Electricity Market. Once that interconnection was lost, the system could no longer remain stable and the entire state experienced what is known as a black system event with parts of the state left without power for about three days.

While this event is much more localised, state MP Sam Tefler said it raises plenty of questions about energy security and about ensuring supply.

“There will be many questions to answer once the immediate response and restoration occurs,” he said.

item.title: WA company fined $15,000 over ‘incredibly dangerous’ battery install
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: An electrical contractor in Western Australia has been fined $15,000 for signing off on an “incredibly dangerous” home battery install where incorrect wiring could back-feed lethal voltages to the grid.
item.content:encoded:
Perth-based solar and battery installer Jijiba Pty Ltd, trading as Universal Solar & Electricals, has been fined $15,000 after pleading guilty to breaching Western Australia’s Electricity (Licensing) Regulations 1991 following prosecution by the state’s Director of Energy Safety. 

Perth Magistrates Court heard a Jijiba employee installed a 20 kW battery system and 5 kW inverter at home in Mandurah in October 2025. The electrician’s test sheet did not have a section to record checks of the battery system, but Jijiba still lodged a notice of completion that declared the work was checked, tested and compliant.   

A Western Power inspection later revealed the battery system was incorrectly wired and could back-feed hazardous voltages to the grid in the event of a network power outage. This was classified as a dangerous defect because anyone working on the grid thinking it was not “live” could receive an electric shock of more than 230 V. 

In court, Magistrate Clare Stanyer described the defect as “incredibly dangerous” and said “a person could have died” due to the high risk to electrical workers. She fined Jijiba $15,000 and also ordered it pay $825 in costs and noted the company’s inadequate systems and the need for testing forms to cover the entire scope of the work. 

Small-scale battery adoption has surged in Western Australia in recent months on the back of the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries Program and the state’s own Residential Battery Scheme. 

As of mid-August, more than 50,000 home batteries with a combined storage capacity of more than 1.1(GWh had been installed across the state.

WA Director of Energy Safety Dan Kearney said it is essential that electricians carry out mandatory checks and tests to ensure their work is safe. 

“This error should have been detected at the testing stage, rather than putting others in danger of serious injury or death,” he said. “People working on the network during an outage would expect the grid to be de-energised when it could in fact be receiving lethal voltages.”

“The buck stops with electrical contractors, who must instil a strong culture of compliance and equip their workers with proper testing procedures and documents.”

item.title: Intium unlocks grid connection for Maryvale solar and battery project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: A new 132 kV overhead transmission line that will connect the large-scale Maryvale solar and battery hybrid project to the national grid in central western New South Wales has been completed well ahead of schedule.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney-headquartered high-voltage infrastructure specialist Intium announced it has completed a new 132 kV transmission line in regional New South Wales (NSW) on budget and about three months ahead of schedule, unlocking a connection point for Gentari’s Maryvale solar and battery project.

The Maryvale project, being built on a 360-hectare site near Wellington in central western NSW, integrates a 243 MWp solar installation with a 172 MW / 409 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS).

The new overhead transmission line, that stretches nine kilometres from Maryvale to network operator Essential Energy’s existing Geurie Zone substation, provides the network connection point required for the Maryvale project to export electricity to the NSW network.

Intium, which delivered the transmission line construction and commissioning program for Essential Energy, installing the 132 kV overhead line with steel and concrete poles and high-capacity fibre, said the project is now complete and awaiting electrification.

“With grid connection delays a persistent bottleneck for renewable projects, the project shows what an end-to-end delivery model can achieve for network operators,” the company said, adding that “this critical network link will support the integration of regional solar and battery storage into the electricity grid and help unlock clean energy generation in the central-west region of NSW.”

The Maryvale solar and battery project, that ranks among Australia’s largest sites using DC-coupled technologies to optimise output and storage management, is expected to commence commercial operations in mid-2027. 

Gentari said the project is designed to enhance system strength and inertia, helping to stabilise the grid and ensure that renewables can be integrated more reliably in an area with already high levels of renewable penetration.

“By combining solar PV with a BESS connected on the DC side of the inverter, Maryvale can capture surplus midday solar, reduce energy losses by avoiding unnecessary AC-DC conversion cycles, and optimise output without increasing its land footprint,” the developer said. “The BESS is capable of firming and smoothing variable solar supply, shifting energy to align with demand, and providing essential grid support services such as Frequency Control Ancillary Services (FCAS).”

“Together, these features position Maryvale as a flexible, grid-strengthening power station tailored for Australia’s modern electricity system.”

The project was one of the first solar-BESS hybrid projects to win a Long Term Energy Storage Agreement (LTESA) through the NSW government auctions.

item.title: Record quarter for renewable capacity committed to construction
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: A record 2.4 GW of large-scale solar, wind, and battery projects were committed to construction across Australia during the third quarter of 2026, marking “significant” progress towards achieving the federal government’s target of 82% renewables by 2030.
item.content:encoded:
Australian renewable energy projects have been committed to construction at an “all-time record” level during Q3 2026 according to the latest update of the Australian Renewable Energy Scorecard from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) and Green Energy Markets (GEM).

The data, compiled and analysed by IEEFA Australia Lead Analyst Electricity Johanna Bowyer and Green Energy Markets Chief Executive Officer Tristan Edis, shows a 2.4 GW jump in large-scale renewable energy projects financed for construction on Australia’s National Electricity Market (NEM) and Western Australia’s South West Interconnected System (SWIS) grids in the July-September quarter.

“This quarter represents an all-time record for renewable energy projects being committed to construction,” the Scorecard reads. “This is 20% up on the previous record (in Q1 2022), and a step change from the low volumes recorded in Q1 and Q2 of this year.”

Wind makes up the lion’s share of new capacity financed for construction in the last quarter, with 1.5 GW committed. Another 910 MW of large-scale solar was committed to construction during the quarter, the second highest on record after the 1.2 GW committed in the April-June quarter.

The Scorecard shows a combined 3.4 GW of solar is currently under construction across the NEM and SWIS while 3.5 GW of wind is being built.

There was also material progress in utility-scale batteries in construction in most states with a combined 29.5 GWh currently being built with projects committed to construction in the July-September quarter adding a further 13%.

The IEEFA/GEM Scorecard notes that the utility-scale batteries in construction would provide 21% of the new energy storage capacity required across Australia’s main grids to achieve the federal government’s target of 82% renewables by 2030.

“Overall, battery projects put into construction this quarter now mean we have 34% of the extra capacity we need to reach 2030 requirements, wind projects 21% of new capacity required, and solar projects 16% of new capacity required,” it reads.

In spite of the record construction commitments during the last quarter, the Scorecard warns that overall utility-scale capacity currently under construction is far short of the additional new capacity required to be operational by 2030.

“The amount of capacity currently under construction is significantly lower than the new capacity that needs to be operational by 2030 to meet the target,” it notes.

Across the solar and wind pipeline, the biggest bottleneck where project progress appears to be stalling is securing a contract for a significant portion of power generated.

“There is a significant lack of renewable energy projects with power purchase agreements (PPAs),” the Scorecard reads. “Only a small percentage of projects that have been fully approved have also been contracted (6% across Australia’s main grids).”

The importance of government support schemes has also been highlighted, with cuts to federal household battery rebates leading to a 44% drop in small-scale battery system installations, and a 20% cut to installation sizes.

The IEEFA/GEM Scorecard also shows rooftop solar installations dropped by 12% in Q3 2026 compared to the record installation levels of Q2 2026, but they remained materially higher than recent year averages. The average size of a rooftop solar system dropped to 9.9 kW, down from 10.5 kW in the previous quarter.

Small-scale battery installations declined by 44% after the record high of Q2 2026 while system sizes were reduced by 20%.

Despite the dropoff, Edis said the small-scale market outlook remains positive.

“While home solar and battery systems have dropped precipitously this quarter, the record high installs over the second quarter of 2026, and rooftop solar still being materially above recent year averages, are cause for optimism,” he said. “Battery installations falling below recent averages, however, shows government support is still needed to help people invest in the long-term savings and security that renewables and battery systems provide.”

item.title: Cutting home battery subsidy shapes as false economics
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australia’s home battery boom has become a victim of its own success. More than 600,000 batteries have now been installed under the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries Program. This extraordinary uptake has surpassed the expectations of the government’s program modelers. With the allocated funds being utilised sooner than expected, the Cheaper Home Batteries Program is now under scrutiny as the government looks for savings.
item.content:encoded:
Focusing only on the cost of the subsidy misses an important part of the equation: home batteries are not simply subsidised appliances sitting in individual homes. At sufficient scale, they are part of Australia’s energy infrastructure.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen recently said batteries are “putting downward pressure on prices for everyone, whether or not you have a battery.” The Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) data points the same way: NEM wholesale prices fell 47% year-on-year in the June 2026 quarter, with lower evening peaks a key driver. Western Australia’s wholesale prices rose over the same period as coal availability tightened, which is exactly why flexible capacity there, including more than 1,000 MWh of household storage, matters.

A battery in a home can still benefit the grid

Nationally, households with batteries are collectively reducing evening demand by hundreds of MW. Importantly, much of that benefit occurs without anyone actively controlling those batteries.

Electricity networks and generators have to be capable of supplying the periods when demand is highest, even if those peaks occur for relatively short periods. If distributed batteries can reduce those peaks, they can reduce the need for additional generation, storage and network capacity over time.

When the government subsidises a battery, it isn’t only helping a household buy an energy product. It is helping build distributed energy capacity.

Seen through that lens, simply cutting the program because uptake has exceeded expectations risks being a false economy.

The program faces a fair question: is it simply subsidising households that could have bought a battery anyway? The Opposition has argued as much. Rewiring Australia compared every postcode and found batteries are being installed in line with each income band’s share of households. About 81% are in postcodes with a median household income of $60,000 to $120,000, almost exactly the share of households living there. Higher-income postcodes have installed slightly more than their share, but not dramatically.

Plico’s data fits: our busiest postcodes since 1 July 2025 are the Perth suburbs of Armadale, Cockburn and Wanneroo, outer-suburban growth corridors. About half of our customers have used the WA no-interest loan, which is only available to households with a combined income under $210,000.

The sharper divide is housing type: postcodes dominated by owner-occupied houses have installed about 6.5 times as many batteries per household as those with mostly strata and rentals. That is an argument for widening access, not winding the program back.

The bigger opportunity is coordination

A battery that can respond to the needs of the electricity system is potentially much more valuable. That is the purpose of a virtual power plant (VPP).

A VPP coordinates thousands of individual batteries so they can operate, when needed, more like a single power station responding collectively to periods of high demand, excess solar generation or other conditions in the electricity market.

Western Australia has already recognised this. Participation in a VPP is a requirement of the WA Residential Battery Scheme, which provides rebates of up to $1,300 for Synergy customers and $3,800 for Horizon Power customers on top of the federal incentive.

Rather than asking whether Australia can afford to keep subsidising batteries, we should be asking how we extract greater public value from the batteries taxpayers are helping households install.

There is a reasonable argument that an open-ended subsidy cannot continue indefinitely.

But there is a significant difference between gradually reducing support as the market matures and withdrawing support before we have captured the system-wide benefits that drove the policy in the first place.

A better approach would be to increasingly connect the subsidy to the capability of batteries to support the grid. That doesn’t necessarily mean compelling householders to hand control of their battery to an energy company whenever it wants it.

Customers need to understand how their battery will be used, how much capacity remains available for their own needs and what they receive in return for participating.

The taxpayer helps a household overcome the upfront cost of a battery, the household receives lower energy costs and greater energy independence, and the electricity system gains flexible capacity that can be called on when it is most valuable.

The next stage of the market needs to be about performance as well as installation.

The objective should not be to maximise the number of batteries registered to a VPP, but to maximise the amount of useful, reliable and consumer-supported flexible capacity available to the energy system.

The extraordinary response to the Cheaper Home Batteries Program suggests consumers are ready to participate. Now policy needs to move to the next phase.

The question shouldn’t be whether the success of the program means we can afford to cut it, rather it should focus on how we turn that success into an energy resource that benefits everybody.

That is an opportunity worth being taken seriously by those decision-makers who are now getting the wobbles.

Author: Robbie Campbell, Chief Executive Officer, Plico

item.title: UNSW researcher wins international award for pioneering PV work
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: UNSW solar researcher Xiaojing Hao has received one of the world’s most prestigious awards for engineers and scientists in recognition of her research and technological contributions to solar energy conversion.
item.content:encoded:
University of New South Wales (UNSW) Scientia Associate Professor Xiaojing Hao, a pioneer in the field of thin-film PV, has been recognised on the international stage as the winner of the Hamakawa Award in recognition of her breakthroughs in developing the next generation of solar energy cells.

The Hamakawa Award honours outstanding contributions to PV research and technological accomplishment. Hao, who has established herself as a world leader in the field of PV technology through the creation of four different thin-film technologies, was presented with the award during the World Conference on PV Energy Conversion staged in South Korea last week.

Hao’s record-breaking research focuses on the development of low-cost, high-efficiency thin-film and tandem solar cells, with a focus on emerging PV materials and scalable device engineering.

Since joining the field as a PhD student in 2006, Hao is credited with driving four different thin-film PV technologies to world-record status, including last month achieving a certified stabilised power conversion efficiency of 23.5% for a 30 x 30cm perovskite submodule. Earlier this year she was part of a team that achieved a certified power conversion efficiency with solar cells made from antimony chalcogenide, an emerging material regarded as a strong candidate for next-generation solar technology.

Hao said she is proud of her team’s work and now hopes to see the next-generation PV technologies she is developing move from the laboratory into fabrication and real-world applications.

“My ambition is to help advance silicon-based tandem solar cells, accelerate the transition to more efficient and sustainable energy technologies, and contribute to global net-zero goals and industrial decarbonisation,” she said.

“This is an incredibly exciting field with the potential to reshape how the world generates and uses energy. We need curious, creative and ambitious students who want to tackle challenges that matter.”

Hao is the first Australian PV scientist to receive the Hamakawa Award and was nominated for the honour by UNSW Scientia Professor Martin Green who cited not only her significant research achievements but also her leadership in the field.

“Xiaojing has greatly surpassed the award criteria by developing not one, but undoubtedly uniquely, four different thin-film PV technologies to world record status,” Green said in the submission.

“She has demonstrated outstanding international leadership in the ongoing development of these technologies.”

“She has made an important and internationally recognised contribution to the development of the global PV sector and helped define pathways to the future.”

The Hamakawa award was established in 2014 as part of the World Conference on PV Energy Conversion. The award is not given every year.

item.title: Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar by 2029 with policy reforms
item.dc:creator: Patrick Jowett
item.description: IESR says Indonesia could achieve most of its 100 GW of solar by 2029 target through coordinated utility-scale procurement, rooftop PV deployment, diesel replacement and rural electrification, but warns regulatory and grid barriers need to be addressed.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s cumulative installed solar capacity reached 1.59 GW as of the first quarter of 2026 (Q1 2026), according to the latest report from the Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR), a Jakarta-based think tank. 

IESR’s Indonesia Solar Energy Outlook 2027 says the figure is equivalent to about 1.5% of Indonesia’s power generation capacity and 0.3% of electricity production.

Rooftop PV currently accounts for the largest share of installed capacity, standing at 0.9 GW as of Q1 2026. Utility-scale solar accounted for 0.33 GW, captive solar for 0.3 GW and installations in remote areas for around 0.06 GW.

With the country passing the 1 GW solar milestone in 2025, IESR said the current growth rate is “far behind the government’s ambition to make solar power one of the backbones of the national energy system”, as set out in the country’s 100 GW solar power program which President Prabowo Subianto has set a target of achieving by 2029.

The program officially launched in August with a first phase of 14 projects totaling about 5.2 GW, but only 526 MW of this capacity currently have targeted completion dates, IESR’s report reveals.

The think tank adds that deployments are currently held back by regulatory gaps, procurement uncertainty and limited grid access.

In a statement sent to pv magazine, IESR CEO Fabby Tumiwa said the 100 GW ambition needs to be reflected in updates to Indonesia’s 2025-2034 electricity supply business plan (RUPTL), with greater emphasis on utility-scale PV and battery energy storage systems (BESS), diesel replacement with solar-plus-storage and rooftop PV deployment.

IESR’s modelling suggests Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar capacity by 2029 if development proceeds through multiple channels simultaneously. 

The report says about 8 GW is already planned through RUPTL and Mentari GigaOne procurements, while a further 56 GW could come through procurements by Indonesia’s state-owned electric utility PLN. It suggests the remaining 33 GW could be developed through rooftop PV, diesel replacement, rural electrification, captive solar and other distributed applications.

IESR said five enablers that must move together – demand, rooftop access, procurement, grid and supply chain – will determine whether the 100 GW scales.

Under a high-electrification scenario, Indonesia’s electricity demand could be around 160 TWh higher in 2035 than under a business-as-usual scenario, according to figures from the report. Electrification of transport, industry, cooling, cooking and data centres, alongside potential electricity exports, could help create additional demand for solar generation.

IESR also suggests rooftop solar quotas be determined according to grid hosting capacity at the substation level, rather than through the current quota system, which it said limits deployment.

For utility-scale projects, the report recommends more transparent procurement schedules and reverse auctions. Projects are frequently tendered individually without a clear timetable, making it harder for developers, lenders and suppliers to prepare, IESR said.

Grid and storage investment will also need to keep pace. Indonesia’s 2025-2034 RUPTL includes 42.6 GW of renewable energy and 10.3 GW of energy storage, but some transmission infrastructure needed to integrate solar is not scheduled until 2030-2034. IESR’s report recommends regulatory changes and incentives to encourage investment in storage.

In the report, Tumiwa notes that Indonesia’s domestic solar supply chain is rising faster than demand. Solar module production capacity reached 27 GW per year in 2026, although the report notes more than half of it needs further verification due to relabelling allegations, while cell capacity now stands at 14.3 GW.

It said that after 98.2% of Indonesia’s solar module exports went to the United States in 2025, US preliminary duties of about 104% in February 2026 cut Indonesian exports to the US by about 98%, from a peak of 2.2 GW in November 2025 to 34 MW in April 2026. Final duties of up to 268% followed in September 2026

IESR said the 100 GW program “could provide a market anchor [for the solar supply chain] if accompanied by consistent policy and project certainty.”

The 100 GW target must also be explicitly incorporated into revisions of the National Electricity General Plan (RUKN) and RUPTL, IESR added, with defined procurement channels, grid requirements, distributed solar roles and legal frameworks for project ownership and financing.

From pv magazine Global
